overview.title: Packaging Process
content: The process of protecting the chips (Dies) cut from the wafer from external physical and chemical shocks, and electrically connecting them to the device circuit board (PCB).
Recently, Advanced Packaging technology, which bundles multiple chips into one, has emerged as a key factor in improving semiconductor performance.

components.name: Dicing Saw
components.desc: Cuts the wafer with a diamond blade to separate it into individual chips.

components.name: Die Bonder
components.desc: Attaches the separated chips to a lead frame or package substrate.

components.name: Wire Bonder
components.desc: Connects the chip's pads to the substrate using gold wire. (Flip Chip bumps are primarily used recently)

components.name: Molding Equipment
components.desc: Encapsulates the entire chip with epoxy molding compound (EMC) to form a protective layer.

principle.title: Operating Principle (Thermal Dissipation Model)
content: One of the important roles of packaging is to effectively dissipate the heat generated by the chip.
The Junction Temperature (Tj) of the chip is determined by adding the product of Power (P) and Thermal Resistance (θJA) to the Ambient Temperature (Ta). (Tj = Ta + P × θJA)
It is essential to design packaging materials and structures that lower thermal resistance.

test.question: What is the correct action to take during the packaging stage to resolve the heating issue of a semiconductor chip?
options: Use materials with high Thermal Resistance.
Use heat sinks or materials with low Thermal Resistance.
Wrap the chip only in air to increase insulation.
test.explanation: The lower the thermal resistance (θJA), the easier it is for the heat generated by the chip to escape to the outside, allowing the junction temperature (Tj) to be maintained within a safe range.

theory.title: 8. Packaging Advanced Theory
content: Packaging is a back-end process that protects the individual chips (Dies) cut from the wafer from external physical impacts, moisture, and corrosion, and electrically, mechanically, and thermally connects them to the system board (PCB).

The basic process consists of 1) Wafer Dicing, 2) Die Attach, which attaches the chip to a lead frame or substrate, 3) Wire Bonding, which connects the chip and the substrate with wires, and 4) Molding, which covers the chip with epoxy molding compound (EMC).

How to dissipate the immense 'heat' generated when the chip operates is a key challenge in packaging design. According to the thermal circuit model, internal junction temperature of the chip (Tj) = external temperature (Ta) + power consumption (P) * thermal resistance (θJA). High-performance chips must have a thermal resistance structure close to 0.

Recently, to overcome the limits of Moore's Law, Flip-Chip technology, which makes bumps on the bottom of the chip and attaches it upside down instead of wires, TSV (Through Silicon Via) technology, which stacks chips vertically by making electrodes that penetrate the silicon chip, and 2.5D/3D Advanced Packaging technologies, which gather various types of chips on a single substrate (Silicon Interposer) to maximize performance, are developing explosively.
